passages.t: A king sends for a seer
passages.happening:
“Then the Israelites traveled on and camped in the plains of Moab near the Jordan, across from Jericho” (verse 1).

Balak, king of Moab, has seen what happened to the Amorites, and Moab is afraid (verses 2-3). He sends messengers a great distance, to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor near the Euphrates. “So please come now and put a curse on this people, because they are too mighty for me” (verse 6).

The elders of Moab and Midian arrive ‘with the fees for divination in hand’ (verse 7). That night God comes to Balaam. “Do not go with them. You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed” (verse 12). Balaam sends the messengers home.

Balak sends more princes, of higher rank, with larger promises (verses 15-17). Balaam answers, “If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything small or great to go beyond the command of the LORD my God” (verse 18). But he asks them to stay the night, to find out ‘what else the LORD has to tell me’ (verse 19). That night God says, ‘get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Israel has reached its last camp before the promised land. It will stay on these plains for the rest of Numbers and all of Deuteronomy.

The three chapters that begin here are unlike anything else in the book. For most of the story Israel is offstage. The people are down in their tents and know nothing. On the hills above them a king and a hired seer are working against them, and God is defending them without their knowledge.

Balak's fear is easy to understand. A large people has arrived on his border, and it has just defeated two kings to his north. The text does not mock him. He does what a king of his world would do. He hires an expert.

In the ancient Near East many people believed that a trained seer could move the gods and bind the future with words. Kings hired such men before battle. A curse was treated as a real weapon. Balak says exactly this: ‘those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed’ (verse 6). The ‘fees for divination’ show that it was a paid profession. Such divination was forbidden in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10).

Balaam was famous. He is one of the few people in the five books of Moses known from outside the Bible. In 1967 an inscription was found at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, written in ink on a plastered wall and usually dated to about the eighth century BC. It tells of a vision given to ‘Balaam son of Beor’, a seer of the gods. It does not describe the events of Numbers. It shows that he was remembered in that region for centuries.

God's first word to Balaam settles the matter before it begins. Israel is already under God's blessing. The word reaches back to God's promise to Abraham: “I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you” (Genesis 12:3). After all the grumbling of the wilderness, a reader might wonder whether that promise still held. God tells a foreign seer that it does.

Balaam is hard to read, and the story means him to be. He uses the name of the LORD. He says fine things about obeying God. Yet after a plain ‘no’ he asks the second group to wait while he inquires again.
passages.later:
The New Testament remembers Balaam as a warning. Peter writes of those who ‘follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness’ (2 Peter 2:15). Jude speaks of ‘the error of Balaam’ (Jude 1:11). Both are warning the church about teachers who serve for gain.

Moses later summed up the whole story in one sentence: “Yet the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam, and the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loves you” (Deuteronomy 23:5).
passages.asks: Israel never knew, that night, that a curse had been ordered against it and refused. Ask what God may have turned away from you that you never heard about. And ask whether, like Balaam, you have gone back to ask again about something on which God's answer was already clear.

passages.happening:
Balaam sets out on his donkey. “Then God’s anger was kindled because Balaam was going along, and the angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose him” (verse 22).

The donkey sees the angel with a drawn sword and turns into a field. Balaam beats her. The angel stands in a narrow way between two vineyard walls. She presses against the wall and crushes Balaam's foot, and he beats her again. The angel stands where there is no room to turn at all. She lies down under him, and he beats her with his staff (verses 23-27).

“Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth, and she said to Balaam, ‘What have I done to you that you have beaten me these three times?’” (verse 28). He answers that if he had a sword he would kill her. She asks, ‘Am I not the donkey you have ridden all your life until today? Have I ever treated you this way before?’ (verse 30).

“Then the LORD opened Balaam’s eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand” (verse 31). The angel says, ‘your way is perverse before me’ (verse 32). Balaam says, “I have sinned,” and offers to go home (verse 34). He is told to go on, ‘but you are to speak only what I tell you’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
The scene is meant to be funny, and its first hearers would have laughed.

Balaam is the famous seer, the man kings pay because he can see what others cannot. On this road he is the only one who cannot see. His donkey sees the angel three times. He threatens to kill her with a sword he does not have, while an angel with a drawn sword stands a few steps in front of him. The man hired to bend the gods with words cannot manage his own animal, and loses an argument to her.

The story is built in threes. The angel stands three times, each time in a tighter place: an open road, a walled lane, a spot with no room to turn. Balaam strikes three times. Step by step his ways out are taken from him.

The Hebrew word for the angel's ‘opposing’ Balaam is satan. Here it is an ordinary noun that means an adversary. It is not a name. Only in later books of the Old Testament does it become the title of a particular accuser.

The donkey was the usual animal for travel, and a good one could serve a man for years, as this one reminds him. Her question is fair, and the angel repeats it. The angel also says that the donkey saved Balaam's life (verse 33). The beast he beat was the one protecting him.

The humor carries the point of the next two chapters. God ‘opened the donkey’s mouth’, and she spoke. Then God ‘opened Balaam’s eyes’. If God can make a donkey speak sense, he can make a hired seer speak a blessing. Balaam will say only what God puts in his mouth, and it will be no more to his credit than her speech was to hers.

Who ‘the angel of the LORD’ is has been understood in two ways. Some Christian readers take him to be an appearance of the Son of God before he became man, because he speaks with God's own authority. Others hold that he is an angel sent as God's messenger. The text does not settle it.
passages.later:
Peter sums up the scene: Balaam ‘was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness’ (2 Peter 2:16).

Proverbs says something the donkey would have agreed with: “A righteous man regards the life of his animal, but the tender mercies of the wicked are only cruelty” (Proverbs 12:10).
passages.hard:
Why does God tell Balaam to go, and then become angry when he goes?

Verse 20 has God say, ‘get up and go with them’. Verse 22 says that God's anger was kindled ‘because Balaam was going along’. Readers explain this in several ways.

One explanation is that the permission had a condition: go, but do only what I tell you. Balaam set out with his heart already on the reward and on finding some way to earn it. The angel calls his way ‘perverse’.

A second is that Balaam should never have asked again. God's first answer was clear (verse 12). By asking a second time he showed that he hoped God would change his mind. God gave him what he wanted, and a warning with it.

A third, held by many critical scholars, is that the story of the donkey was once a separate tradition and was placed here, which would explain the tension. Even on this view the finished text asks the reader to see a gap between what Balaam says and what he wants.

The New Testament's verdict leans toward the first two. It remembers him as one ‘who loved the wages of wickedness’ (2 Peter 2:15), though in this chapter he says all the right things. A person can use the right words about obeying God while wanting something else.

Did a donkey really speak? Christians who take the account as history note that the text says plainly that the LORD opened her mouth, as he later opened Balaam's eyes. Others read the episode as a story told with deliberate humor to make its point. On either reading the point is the one given above.
passages.asks: Balaam was stopped three times and took each one for an obstacle. Ask what has blocked your way lately, and whether you have asked if it might be a mercy. And ask whether there is anything you say you will do only if God allows, while hoping that he will.

passages.happening:
Balak comes out to meet Balaam at the border and reproaches him for the delay. “Am I really not able to richly reward you?” (verse 37).

Balaam answers, “See, I have come to you,” and then, ‘can I say just anything? I must speak only the word that God puts in my mouth’ (verse 38).

Balak offers sacrifices. The next morning he takes Balaam up to Bamoth-baal. “From there he could see the outskirts of the camp of the people” (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
The king and the seer meet at last, and at once they are at cross purposes. Balak thinks the matter is one of price. He has the money, so he expects the curse. Balaam has just learned on the road that he is not his own master in this.

His sentence in verse 38 is the key line of the whole story. It has been said three times in this chapter, in slightly different words (verses 20, 35, 38). The reader is being made ready. Whatever comes out of this man's mouth in the next two chapters will be God's word and not his own.

Bamoth-baal was a height on the edge of the high plain, and its name carries the name of the god Baal. Balak takes Balaam where the edge of Israel's camp is in view, so that the seer can look at the people he is to curse.

The view is worth a thought. Far below lie the tents set out in the order of chapter 2, tribe by tribe around the tabernacle. The people in them know nothing of the two men on the height. The rest of the story is God's care for people who do not know they need it.
passages.later:
The prophet Micah, centuries later, told Israel to remember this very thing: “My people, remember what Balak king of Moab counseled and what Balaam son of Beor answered” (Micah 6:5).

A psalm says of God's watch over his people, “Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4).
passages.asks: Balak assumed that enough money would buy the words he wanted. Ask where you assume that everything has its price, and what cannot be bought. And ask whether you speak, in your work or your church, the word you believe God has given, or the word that the person paying wants to hear.
